statement: The thousand years symbolise the fullness of Christ's reign now (ten cubed: completeness). It began when the Lamb who was slain took the throne, and believers reign with him as those seated with Christ in the heavenly places. It is not a future earthly era to wait for but the present reality of the kingdom.
note: Proponents stress the believer's present reign in Christ more than the heavenly reign of departed saints. Those who expect the gospel's growing triumph also lean toward the present-progressive stance.

statement: The accuser was cast down and bound by the cross: Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them, and the strong man is bound so his house can be plundered. Satan's power now is chiefly deception, a lie about identity, which loses its hold where the truth of Christ is seen.
note: Revelation 12 (the accuser thrown down) and Revelation 20 (the dragon bound) are read as two pictures of the cross's victory.

statement: The first resurrection is the new birth: being raised with Christ from spiritual death into union with him. Those who share in it reign with him now, and over them 'the second death has no power'.

Christ's appearing will consummate what the cross accomplished, bringing the resurrection, the judgment and the fullness of the new creation together. The view emphasises that Christ already 'comes' to his people by the Spirit, and that the final appearing completes a victory already won rather than starting one.
note: Many 'coming' texts (for example the clouds of Revelation 1:7, or the 'coming' to churches in Revelation 2–3) are read as present or first-century comings in judgment and grace. A minority within the broader movement leans toward fully realised readings, which most proponents reject.

statement: The view rejects a separate escape from a future tribulation as a fear-based framework. Believers are already 'caught up' in the sense of being seated with Christ, and they will be gathered to him at his one appearing.
note: Proponents give the question little weight: the believer's security rests on union with Christ, not on a timetable.

statement: The 'great tribulation' of the Olivet Discourse fell on the old covenant order in the Jewish War and the destruction of the temple in AD 70. In Revelation, tribulation is also the ongoing experience of believers who share in Christ's suffering and kingdom (Revelation 1:9), and they overcome it by the blood of the Lamb, not by fear.
note: Preterist-leaning proponents tie the tribulation to AD 66-70; idealist-leaning proponents treat it as a pattern throughout the age. Almost all reject a future seven-year tribulation as the book's centre.

statement: 'Antichrist' is above all a spirit and a mindset: whatever denies that Christ has come in the flesh and puts something in his place. The beasts picture the power of the flesh, persecuting rule and false religion. The mark on the hand and forehead is a life and mind shaped by fear and self-effort, set against the Father's name on the forehead.
note: Many accept a first-century referent (Nero, the persecuting empire) as the first layer of the symbol, and read 666 as the number of humanity, falling short of God's seventh-day rest.

statement: 'This generation' meant Jesus' hearers: the shaking of the old covenant world and the temple's fall were fulfilled by AD 70, making way for the new covenant kingdom that cannot be shaken. The final consummation remains Christ's to bring.
note: Some proponents read the whole discourse in idealist terms instead (contemporaries-dual).

statement: Daniel's seventy weeks are fulfilled in Christ: he finished transgression, made an end of sin, brought in everlasting righteousness and confirmed the new covenant by his death. The seventieth week is about the Messiah, not a future Antichrist.

The date is secondary because the unveiling of Christ speaks to every generation. Proponents with a covenantal emphasis tend to favour an early (pre-70) date. The date of Revelation is disputed among scholars.
note: Preterist-leaning proponents favour the early date; others are content with c. AD 95.

statement: The true Israel, the Bride and the New Jerusalem are the one people of God, Jew and Gentile, in union with Christ. The 144,000 (twelve times twelve times a thousand) and the innumerable multitude are two views of the same complete people.
note: Some proponents also expect many Jewish people to come to faith in Christ, without a separate national programme.

statement: Because the decisive battle is already won, the church reads history from victory: the Rider on the white horse conquers by his word, and the harvest of Revelation 14 is the fruit of the gospel. The leaven of the kingdom is expected to work through the whole lump.
note: Proponents are uniformly hopeful and anti-fear, but some hold the amillennial 'realistic' expectation that wheat and tares grow together until the end.

statement: The kingdom is present now, within and among believers, as Christ reigns from the throne and his people reign in life through grace. It grows as minds are renewed and the gospel spreads, and it is consummated in the new heavens and new earth.
note: Amillennial-leaning proponents place the emphasis on inaugurated-consummated (already/not yet) rather than progressive growth.

statement: Judgment centres on the cross, where the world's sin was judged and the ruler of this world cast out. A final judgment at Christ's appearing completes it, with the books opened and death and Hades themselves thrown into the lake of fire.
note: Within the view the lake of fire is read in different ways: as eternal judgment, as the final destruction of all that opposes life, or as purifying fire. Proponents present it with care rather than as a tool of fear.

statement: The view's roots lie in the spiritual exegesis of Alexandria, Tyconius and Augustine, whose present-reign, two-cities reading of Revelation dominated the church for a millennium. Its distinctive modern form, emphasising the finished work, union with Christ and the renewed mind, has grown since the late twentieth century.
note: No stance fits exactly: the Augustinian stream supplies the view's historical weight, but its modern finished-work form is recent.
